conceptTag: Take the job that pays less but teaches more?
readerTitle: Take the job that pays less but teaches more?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (배관공 견습 졸업생, 식료품 체인 부점장) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 덜 주는 일자리의 임금 차이는 '수업료'다. 그 수업료로 무엇을 배우고 어떤 문이 열리는지 따져 보면 판단이 선다.
misconception: 돈을 더 주는 일이 언제나 더 좋은 선택이다. 또는 반대로, 배움이 있다면 낮은 급여는 무조건 감수할 가치가 있다.

sources.text: 단기·장기 트레이드오프와 선택권(optionality)의 일반적인 의사결정 개념
모든 인물과 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Daniel 사례: $68,000 − $58,000 = 연 $10,000 차이. 모든 수치는 가상입니다.
배관 자격·면허 요건은 국가와 지역마다 다르므로 특정 제도를 언급하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Two offers, one plumber, a $6 gap.
body: Maya just finished her plumbing apprenticeship. A large builder offers $32 an hour to fit the same bathrooms in new apartment blocks, all day, every day.
A small local firm offers $26. The owner fixes old homes, writes his own quotes and wants someone to learn the whole business.

image.label: A young plumber between two job offers
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 공구 가방을 든 젊은 여성 배관공이 갈림길에 서 있음. 왼쪽은 똑같은 욕실이 줄지어 있는 신축 건물, 오른쪽은 오래된 주택 앞 작은 밴과 나이 든 사장님. 각 길 위에 "$32/hr", "$26/hr" 표지판. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: What should Maya weigh first?
body: She has no debt and modest savings. She thinks she might want her own firm one day, but she isn't sure.
Before picking, what's the most useful question?

options.text: Which job pays more right now?
options.feedback: It's the easiest number to see, so it wins by default. But it ignores the **short-term vs long-term trade-off**: what each job makes her worth in five years.

options.text: Which job teaches more? Learning always wins.
options.feedback: Closer, but "always" skips the price. Learning is worth paying for only if she knows what she's buying and can afford it.

options.text: What will each job let her do in five years, and what does the gap cost?
options.feedback: This puts today's pay and tomorrow's skills on the same table. That's the **short-term vs long-term trade-off** at work.

cards.title: Put a price on the lesson.
body: Treat the pay gap as tuition. **$24,000** is what two years at the small firm costs her. The question is what it buys.

breakdown.label: Planned stay
breakdown.detail: Long enough to learn the whole job

cards.eyebrow: Concept at work · Short vs long term
cards.title: The cheap job can be the expensive one.
body: At the builder, Maya gets faster at one task. Her pay rises slowly, and her skills stay narrow.
At the small firm, she learns to find leaks in old pipes, price a job, talk to anxious homeowners and chase unpaid bills. Those skills pay off later, when she charges for whole jobs instead of hours.
The **short-term vs long-term trade-off** asks one thing: is the later payoff likely to be bigger than the $24,000 she gives up now?

cards.title: One job deepens a path. The other opens doors.
body: Maya isn't sure she wants her own firm. That uncertainty is exactly why **optionality** matters: keeping several good futures open is worth more when you can't yet tell which one you'll want.
After two years at the small firm, she could run her own business, work as an estimator or supervise a crew. After two years at the builder, she has mostly one option: more of the same.

image.label: One corridor with one door vs one with four doors
image.brief: 두 개의 복도 비교. 왼쪽 복도 끝에는 문 하나("Same job, faster"), 오른쪽 복도에는 문 네 개("Own firm", "Estimator", "Crew lead", "Same job"). 오른쪽이 더 밝게.

cards.softwareNote: The same choice faces an engineer picking between a well-paid role maintaining one old system and a lower-paid early-stage role touching product, customers and pricing. The second role costs money now but opens more doors later.

cards.title: Now it's a grocery store.
body: Daniel is an assistant manager at a grocery chain. He's offered store manager at $68,000. A regional food distributor offers him a junior buyer role at $58,000, learning supplier deals, pricing and stock planning.
He'd like to open a specialty food shop someday. What should he do?

options.text: Take the store manager job. $10,000 more and a bigger title.
options.feedback: He gains pay and runs a store, which is useful. But he'd skip buying and supplier skills, the part of retail he knows least and needs most for his own shop.

options.text: Take the buyer job, and write down what he must be able to do in 18 months
options.feedback: He pays $10,000 a year for skills that keep more futures open. That's **optionality**. The checkpoint makes sure the learning is real.

options.text: Turn both down and wait for a buyer job that pays $68,000
options.feedback: It looks like having it both ways. But waiting has a cost too, and the offer he wants may never come.

cards.softwareNote: Daniel's choice has a digital twin: a well-paid support lead role vs a lower-paid product role at a small startup that teaches pricing and customer research.

cards.title: "Teaches more" is a promise, not a fact.
body: Ask who will teach you, how often, and whether you'll do the work or just watch. A busy owner may hand you the same three tasks forever.
Check what you can afford. If a pay cut means new debt, it can close doors instead of opening them.
And learning slows. Set a date to ask: am I still paying tuition, or just earning less?

image.label: A calendar with a checkpoint circled
image.brief: 벽에 걸린 달력. 18개월 뒤 날짜에 빨간 동그라미와 "Still learning?" 메모. 옆에 작은 돼지 저금통. 단순한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Maya's learning has slowed.
body: A year in, Maya can quote jobs and handle customers. Lately she mostly does routine repairs. The builder still wants her, now at $34 an hour.

options.text: Stay. She's comfortable and the owner likes her.
options.feedback: Comfort feels free, but she's still paying $8 an hour of tuition for lessons that have mostly stopped. The **long-term trade-off** no longer favors staying as is.

options.text: Ask the owner to let her run bookings and hire help, with a review in six months
options.feedback: She keeps building the skills that widen her options and gives the job a clear test. If he says no, she has her answer.

options.text: Go to the builder now. She's learned enough.
options.feedback: The pay is better and her new skills travel with her. But she may be leaving before the parts that matter most for her own firm.

cards.title: A lower salary is tuition. Know what it buys.
body: You used two ideas: the **short-term vs long-term trade-off** to price the pay gap against future earnings, and **optionality** to count the doors each job opens.
**Try it today:** think of a role you or someone on your team is weighing. Write the yearly pay gap and three things it would let you do in five years.
